# Introduction

## Purpose of the Assignment

This study note reviews confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using the UCLA seminar *Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) in R with lavaan*. The goal is to understand how observed questionnaire items measure latent constructs, specify and identify measurement models, evaluate model fit, and compare competing models. The R code below is designed to be reproducible once the UCLA SAQ-8 dataset has been downloaded into the project folder.

## Confirmatory Factor Analysis and Exploratory Factor Analysis

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) investigates possible factor structures without requiring a fully specified pattern of item-factor relationships. CFA tests a theory-driven structure specified in advance. In CFA, the researcher states which indicators load on each latent factor and then evaluates whether the resulting model reproduces the observed covariance matrix adequately.

# Data and Software

## Required Packages

Install `haven` and `lavaan` once in the RStudio Console using `install.packages(c("haven", "lavaan"))`.

```{r}
library(haven)
library(lavaan)
```

## Importing the SAQ-8 Data

Download the SAQ-8 data from the [UCLA seminar](https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/seminars/rcfa/) and save it in this project's folder. The following chunk looks for common formats and stops with a clear message if no file is present. Set `data_file` manually if your download has a different filename.

```{r}
files <- list.files(pattern = "\\.(sav|csv|dta)$", ignore.case = TRUE)
if (length(files) == 0) stop("Download the UCLA SAQ-8 dataset (.sav, .csv, or .dta) into this folder before rendering.")
data_file <- files[1]
ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(data_file))
saq <- switch(ext,
  sav = as.data.frame(read_sav(data_file)),
  dta = as.data.frame(read_dta(data_file)),
  csv = read.csv(data_file))
names(saq) <- tolower(names(saq))
items <- sprintf("q%02d", 1:8)
if (!all(items %in% names(saq))) {
  stop(paste("Expected q01 through q08; available columns:", paste(names(saq), collapse = ", "), ". Check the UCLA variable names."))
}
saq_items <- saq[, items]
saq_items[] <- lapply(saq_items, function(x) as.numeric(x))
```

## Examining the Data

```{r}
str(saq_items)
head(saq_items)
summary(saq_items)
round(cor(saq_items, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)
round(cov(saq_items, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)
```

The correlation matrix shows which items tend to move together. Positive correlations suggest that higher responses on one item are associated with higher responses on another. Correlations alone do not prove a particular factor structure; CFA evaluates the entire covariance pattern against a specified model.

# CFA Concepts

## Observed Indicators and Latent Factors

The eight questionnaire responses (`q01` through `q08`) are observed indicators. A latent factor is a construct inferred from their shared covariance rather than measured directly. A factor loading describes how strongly an indicator is associated with its factor, and residual variance represents variation not explained by the factor.

## The Measurement Model

For an indicator $y_i$, a simple measurement equation is $y_i = \\lambda_i\\eta + \\epsilon_i$, where $\\lambda_i$ is the factor loading, $\\eta$ is the latent factor, and $\\epsilon_i$ is the residual. The model-implied covariance matrix is $\\Sigma(\\theta)=\\Lambda\\Phi\\Lambda' + \\Theta$ when residual covariances are modeled in $\\Theta$.

## Path Diagrams

In a CFA path diagram, latent factors are commonly shown as circles or ellipses and measured indicators as rectangles. Single-headed arrows from factors to items represent loadings; double-headed arrows indicate variances or covariances.

## Model Identification and Degrees of Freedom

For $p$ observed variables, the covariance matrix contains $p(p+1)/2$ unique variance/covariance values. Degrees of freedom are the number of unique observed covariance statistics minus the number of freely estimated parameters, under the usual regularity conditions. For three indicators there are $3(4)/2=6$ observed values. A standard one-factor model with one loading fixed, two freely estimated loadings, three residual variances, and one factor variance has six free parameters, giving $df=0$. It is just-identified and cannot be rejected on overall covariance fit alone. Negative degrees of freedom signal insufficient observed information, although nonnegative degrees of freedom alone do not guarantee identification.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Fixed parameter | Assigned a known value, such as a marker loading of 1. |
| Free parameter | Estimated from the data. |
| Under-identified | Parameters cannot be uniquely recovered from observed information. |
| Just-identified | Typically has zero degrees of freedom and reproduces the covariance matrix exactly. |
| Over-identified | Has positive degrees of freedom, allowing testable model restrictions. |

# One-Factor CFA

## Three-Item Model

The lavaan statement `f =~ q03 + q04 + q05` defines one latent factor `f` measured by three observed items. By default, lavaan fixes the first loading to 1 to establish the factor's scale (marker-variable method).

```{r}
m1a <- 'f =~ q03 + q04 + q05'
fit1a <- cfa(m1a, data = saq_items, missing = "fiml")
summary(fit1a, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
standardizedSolution(fit1a)
```

## Variance Standardization

Alternatively, the first loading can be freed and the factor variance fixed at 1. These are different scaling conventions for the same basic measurement structure; their unstandardized coefficients differ, while equivalent model fit and standardized solutions should agree.

```{r}
m1b <- '
 f =~ NA*q03 + q04 + q05
 f ~~ 1*f
'
fit1b <- cfa(m1b, data = saq_items, missing = "fiml")
summary(fit1b, standardized = TRUE)
```

## Standardized Loadings, Residuals, and Implied Covariance

```{r}
subset(standardizedSolution(fit1a), op %in% c("=~", "~~"))
inspect(fit1a, "sigma.hat")
```

A standardized loading closer to 1 in magnitude generally indicates a stronger relationship between the item and factor. A larger standardized residual variance means more item variance remains unexplained. Because the three-item model is just-identified, perfect overall fit does not establish that the substantive theory is correct.

## Eight-Item Model

```{r}
m8 <- 'general =~ q01 + q02 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q06 + q07 + q08'
fit8 <- cfa(m8, data = saq_items, missing = "fiml")
summary(fit8, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
round(fitMeasures(fit8, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr")), 3)
subset(standardizedSolution(fit8), op == "=~")
subset(standardizedSolution(fit8), op == "~~" & lhs == rhs)
```

The chi-square statistic tests exact fit and can be sensitive to sample size. CFI and TLI compare the model with a baseline model (higher values generally indicate better fit). RMSEA assesses approximate misfit per degree of freedom and SRMR summarizes standardized residual discrepancies (lower values generally indicate better fit). Common heuristic benchmarks include CFI/TLI near or above .95 and RMSEA/SRMR near or below .06/.08, but they are not universal decision rules. Model fit must be considered with theoretical plausibility, parameter estimates, sample size, and data characteristics.

# Two-Factor CFA

## Uncorrelated Factors

The following is an illustrative 4+4 split, **not a claim about UCLA's exact item grouping**. Verify the grouping against the seminar and modify it if needed.

```{r}
two_uncorrelated <- '
 factor1 =~ q01 + q02 + q03 + q04
 factor2 =~ q05 + q06 + q07 + q08
 factor1 ~~ 0*factor2
'
fit2u <- cfa(two_uncorrelated, data = saq_items, missing = "fiml")
summary(fit2u, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
```

## Correlated Factors

```{r}
two_correlated <- '
 factor1 =~ q01 + q02 + q03 + q04
 factor2 =~ q05 + q06 + q07 + q08
'
fit2c <- cfa(two_correlated, data = saq_items, missing = "fiml")
summary(fit2c, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
subset(standardizedSolution(fit2c), op == "~~" & lhs != rhs)
```

The correlated model estimates the covariance between the two factors; the uncorrelated model constrains it to zero. A substantial factor correlation suggests the constructs share variation, but does not by itself imply they are identical.

## Model Comparison

```{r}
fits <- list(one_factor = fit8, two_uncorrelated = fit2u, two_correlated = fit2c)
round(t(sapply(fits, fitMeasures, fit.measures = c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr", "aic"))), 3)
lavTestLRT(fit2u, fit2c)
```

Interpret the comparison only after reviewing the output. Prefer a model that has defensible theory, reasonable loadings, acceptable overall fit, and no serious estimation problems. The nested likelihood-ratio test compares the two-factor models when its assumptions are met.

# Second-Order CFA

A second-order factor accounts for correlations among first-order factors. At least three well-measured first-order factors are ordinarily needed for a straightforward identified second-order structure; with only two, extra identifying constraints are typically necessary. The following *illustrative* three-first-order-factor specification is provided for study and should be aligned with the seminar's actual model before treating it as a reproduction.

```{r}
second_order <- '
 F1 =~ q01 + q02 + q03
 F2 =~ q04 + q05 + q06
 F3 =~ q07 + q08
 G =~ F1 + F2 + F3
'
# A two-indicator first-order factor may require additional identification checks.
# This model is an illustration only; review warnings and the UCLA specification.
fit_second <- tryCatch(cfa(second_order, data = saq_items, missing = "fiml"), error = function(e) e)
if (inherits(fit_second, "lavaan")) {
  summary(fit_second, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
} else {
  message("Second-order illustration requires revision: ", conditionMessage(fit_second))
}
```

A second-order loading quantifies the relationship between the general higher-order construct and each first-order factor. A higher-order model is defensible only if both the theory and estimation results support it; do not infer superiority merely from the presence of a general factor.

# Practice Questions and Answers

## 1. What is the difference between exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis?

EFA explores possible latent dimensions and item loading patterns. CFA tests a prespecified measurement structure against observed data. CFA is most appropriate when substantive theory provides clear hypotheses about item-factor relationships.

## 2. What are the observed indicators and latent factors in the SAQ-8 example?

The observed indicators are the eight questionnaire item responses, labeled `q01` to `q08` in this note. The latent factors are the unobserved constructs specified by the researcher; their number and interpretation depend on the model being tested. The exact substantive factor labels should be verified against the UCLA seminar.

## 3. What do factor loadings represent?

Factor loadings describe the expected relationship between a latent factor and an observed item. A standardized loading indicates how many standard deviations the item is expected to change for a one-standard-deviation change in the factor, holding the specified measurement structure constant.

## 4. What do residual variances represent?

Residual variances represent variation in an observed item that is not explained by its modeled latent factor or factors. They can reflect item-specific content, measurement error, and omitted influences.

## 5. How many unique variances and covariances are available for a model with three observed indicators?

There are $p(p+1)/2 = 3(4)/2 = 6$ unique values: three variances and three covariances.

## 6. What is the difference between a fixed parameter and a free parameter?

A fixed parameter is assigned a value before estimation, while a free parameter is estimated from the sample. Fixing one factor loading to 1 is a common way to define a latent factor's scale.

## 7. Why is a model with negative degrees of freedom under-identified?

Negative degrees of freedom indicate more free parameters than unique observed covariance statistics, so the covariance data cannot uniquely determine all of those parameters. Nonnegative degrees of freedom do not automatically guarantee identification.

## 8. Why does fixing one loading and setting residual covariances to zero help identify a model?

Fixing one loading establishes the arbitrary scale of a latent factor. Constraining residual covariances to zero reduces the number of unknown parameters and imposes a testable assumption of local independence conditional on the factors.

## 9. What is the difference between a just-identified model and an over-identified model?

A just-identified model has zero degrees of freedom and generally reproduces the observed covariance matrix exactly, leaving no degrees of freedom for an overall fit test. An over-identified model has positive degrees of freedom and imposes restrictions that can be tested against the data.

## 10. How should chi-square, CFI, TLI, and RMSEA be interpreted?

Chi-square assesses the discrepancy between observed and model-implied covariances under an exact-fit null hypothesis. CFI and TLI assess comparative fit relative to a baseline model, while RMSEA assesses approximate discrepancy adjusted for degrees of freedom. They should be interpreted together with SRMR, loadings, theory, sample size, and possible misspecification rather than using a single rigid cutoff.

## 11. What is the difference between correlated and uncorrelated factors?

Correlated factors are permitted to covary, so they can share variance. Uncorrelated factors have their covariance fixed at zero, imposing a stronger assumption of no linear association between the latent constructs.

## 12. What does a second-order factor represent?

A second-order factor is a higher-level latent construct proposed to explain the shared variation among multiple first-order latent factors. It offers a hierarchical interpretation of the measurement structure.

## 13. Which model appears most theoretically and statistically appropriate based on the results?

A defensible selection requires the actual fitted output and the intended SAQ-8 item-to-factor theory. After rendering with the UCLA dataset, compare fit indices, standardized loadings, residuals, factor correlations, and any warnings. Without those observed results, claiming that one model wins would be unsupported.

## 14. What additional information would you want before making a final decision about the measurement model?

I would examine the sample size and recruitment, missing-data mechanism, item response distributions, the questionnaire's substantive design, alternative theoretically plausible item groupings, local residuals, and whether the proposed structure replicates in an independent sample.

# Summary of Important Lessons

CFA is a theory-guided way to evaluate how observed indicators represent latent constructs. Identification and factor scaling are prerequisites for meaningful estimation. Standardized loadings, residual variances, and several fit indices together inform measurement-model evaluation. Different models should be compared based on both statistical evidence and substantive theory, not fit thresholds alone.
